name: Stinging nettle
summary: A colony-forming perennial of rich, damp ground; its young shoots have a documented cooked-food use.
marks: Opposite, sharply toothed leaves with pointed tips.
Stinging hairs on leaves and stems; observe without touching.
Small greenish flowers in clusters at leaf joints.
range: Widespread in temperate areas; the nettle complex includes native and introduced populations. Confirm the local taxon.
season: Study fresh spring growth and later regrowth; the stage of the shoot matters more than the month.
preparation: Handle with gloves and tongs. Cook identified young shoots; cooking removes the sting.
caution: A sting is not an identification test. Do not eat raw stinging foliage.

lookalikes.name: Other nettles
lookalikes.note: Related nettles differ in leaf arrangement and range. Use a local botanical key.

stewardship: Leave flowering stems and most of the patch for insects. Clip scattered shoots without uprooting.

name: Dandelion
summary: A familiar rosette plant with food uses for its leaves, flowers and roasted roots.
marks: Toothed leaves form a basal rosette.
Each leafless, hollow, unbranched stalk carries one yellow flower head.
Milky sap and a round seed head; neither feature alone proves identity.
range: Eurasian origin; widespread introductions. Taraxacum contains difficult species groups.
season: Young leaves during fresh growth; flowers at full opening. Root gathering destroys the plant.
preparation: Use confirmed leaves and flowers in food; roots have a roasted beverage use.
caution: Sap may irritate skin. Food use does not establish the safety or effectiveness of concentrated products.

lookalikes.name: Other yellow daisies
lookalikes.note: Check the entire rosette and unbranched flower stalk; yellow flowers alone are insufficient.

stewardship: Choose unsprayed ground and leave flowering plants for pollinators.

name: Common yarrow
summary: A meadow perennial with finely divided foliage and clusters of miniature daisy heads.
marks: Featherlike, deeply divided leaves; upper leaves alternate.
Flat clusters consist of tiny daisy heads, with ray and disc florets.
Upright flowering stems arise above the leafy base.
range: Temperate Europe, Asia and North America; cultivated forms and related taxa vary.
season: Observe a flowering plant in the local warm season before studying vegetative specimens.
preparation: Included for identification, flowers and documented traditional use; no medicinal preparation is supplied.
caution: Can cause contact dermatitis. Do not identify by a flat white flower cluster alone.

lookalikes.name: Poison hemlock
lookalikes.note: Hemlock has true umbels of individual flowers. Confirm flower structure and foliage together.

stewardship: Leave most flower heads for pollinators and seed.

name: Black elder
summary: A woody elder whose flowers and properly prepared ripe berries have culinary uses.
marks: Opposite compound leaves with toothed leaflets.
Broad cream flower clusters on woody branches.
Ripe fruit is blue-black; fruit color alone cannot identify an elder.
range: Native to Europe in the cited profile. Other regions have different Sambucus species.
season: Flowers when fully open; berries only after full ripening later in the growing season.
preparation: Flowers are used in cordials. Separate and cook ripe berries using a tested recipe.
caution: Raw or unripe berries and leaves or stems contain cyanide-producing substances. Do not use them.

lookalikes.name: Other elders
lookalikes.note: Verify the species; common names and dark berries do not make elders interchangeable.

lookalikes.name: Poison hemlock
lookalikes.note: Check for a woody shrub and opposite compound leaves, not just white flowers.

stewardship: Leave abundant flowers and fruit for birds and regeneration.

name: American wild mint
summary: An aromatic wet-ground mint that needs species-level checking before any kitchen use.
marks: Opposite, toothed leaves on square stems.
Separated flower whorls at leaf joints, mostly subtended by normal leaves.
Mint scent supports a botanical key; it cannot replace one.
range: North American populations are described by Go Botany; related Asian and European mint names need local verification.
season: Study flowering shoots during active growth. Avoid deciding among mints from young leaves alone.
preparation: Confirm the local species with an experienced botanist before using a wild mint as a tea or flavoring.
caution: Pennyroyal is also a mint and is harmful if eaten. Hybrids complicate identification.

lookalikes.name: Pennyroyal
lookalikes.note: Aromatic foliage and flower whorls occur in both. Use a full regional key.

lookalikes.name: Spearmint
lookalikes.note: Spearmint has more crowded terminal flower spikes with reduced bracts.

stewardship: Protect soft stream banks; grow a correctly named culinary mint when identification is uncertain.

name: Red clover
summary: A common forage legume with pink flower heads; herbal products have separate safety questions.
marks: Three leaflets, often bearing pale chevrons.
Rounded heads of many narrow pink to purple flowers.
Hairy stems and leaf stalks; leaflets commonly sit just below the flower head.
range: Eurasian origin; extensively cultivated and introduced in temperate regions.
season: Study newly opened heads in an unsprayed meadow during the local flowering season.
preparation: A documented food and herbal-use plant; this guide does not provide extracts or treatment recipes.
caution: Check with a clinician before herbal use, especially during pregnancy, breastfeeding or when taking medicines.

lookalikes.name: Other clovers
lookalikes.note: Leaflets and flower-head color vary between species; never use a leaf chevron as a sole test.

stewardship: Leave most heads for pollinators. Avoid agricultural spraying and livestock contamination.

name: Greater plantain
summary: A broad-leaved rosette plant of compacted ground, with documented use of young leaves as cooked greens.
marks: Broad leaves arise from a basal rosette.
Several strong ribs run from the leaf base toward the tip.
Leafless stalks carry narrow spikes of inconspicuous flowers and seeds.
range: Eurasian origin; introduced widely, including eastern North America.
season: Look for young, intact leaves during fresh growth; flowering spikes help confirm the plant.
preparation: Confirmed young leaves can be cooked as greens.
caution: Road margins, sprayed paths and pet-used lawns are poor gathering sites.

lookalikes.name: Other Plantago
lookalikes.note: Ribwort plantain has much narrower leaves. Confirm species rather than relying on the word plantain.

stewardship: Take individual leaves and leave the central growing point intact.

name: Mugwort
summary: An aromatic perennial included for botanical study and the history of herbal practice.
marks: Alternate, deeply lobed leaves.
Leaf undersides are conspicuously pale and hairy.
Small rayless flower heads on branching upper stems.
range: Temperate Eurasia, North Africa and Alaska; introduced elsewhere. Other Artemisia species differ.
season: Observe leaves and mature flower heads through the local growing season.
preparation: No ingestion, burning or medicinal preparation is recommended here.
caution: NCCIH advises against use during pregnancy. Evidence for claimed health effects is limited.

lookalikes.name: Other Artemisia
lookalikes.note: Similar aromatic species vary chemically. Silvery foliage is not enough for identification.

stewardship: Learn whether it is invasive locally; follow land-manager guidance before removing plants.

name: Dog rose
summary: A scrambling rose with hooked prickles and red hips that persist into the cooler season.
marks: Arching branches with strongly hooked prickles.
Alternate compound leaves with toothed leaflets.
Five-petaled pink or white flowers followed by oval red hips.
range: The cited field account covers Britain; use a regional flora for roses elsewhere.
season: Flowers in the local late spring or summer; hips only when fully ripe.
preparation: Hips have a syrup use. Remove or carefully strain out the irritating internal hairs.
caution: Wild roses are difficult to separate. Avoid ornamental shrubs with an unknown spray history.

lookalikes.name: Other wild roses
lookalikes.note: Downy roses and escaped garden species can resemble dog rose; check prickles, leaf hairs and hips.

stewardship: Leave plentiful hips for birds. Take only a small share from an abundant stand.

name: Lemon balm
summary: A cultivated and escaped mint-family herb with wrinkled leaves and a lemon fragrance.
marks: Opposite, oval, softly wrinkled leaves with rounded teeth.
Square stems that become firmer with age.
Small white two-lipped flowers at upper leaf joints.
range: Southern European origin; garden escapes occur beyond its native area.
season: Tender leafy growth before or near the start of flowering.
preparation: Leaves and flowers have a culinary flavoring and tea use. Dry tender leaves promptly with good airflow.
caution: Scent alone does not identify a plant. Confirm leaf arrangement and flowers as well.

lookalikes.name: Other aromatic mints
lookalikes.note: Use a botanical key; lemon scent appears in unrelated plants too.

stewardship: Prefer a known garden plant. Ask permission and leave enough leafy growth for recovery.

name: German chamomile
summary: An annual daisy used for flower tea, distinct from Roman chamomile and other similar daisies.
marks: Finely divided, threadlike leaf segments.
White rays surround a raised yellow central disc.
Confirm the hollow receptacle with a regional key.
range: Temperate Eurasia to Indochina; widely cultivated beyond this range.
season: Fully open flower heads in dry conditions during the local flowering season.
preparation: Use correctly identified flowers for ordinary food or tea preparations.
caution: Allergic reactions can be severe, especially with daisy-family allergies. Medicine interactions are possible.

lookalikes.name: Other chamomiles and mayweeds
lookalikes.note: Similar white daisies require checking leaf, scent and receptacle characters together.

stewardship: Grow a named culinary plant and leave some flower heads for seed.

name: Calendula
summary: A garden annual valued for orange or yellow flower heads and culinary petals.
marks: Oblong to lance-shaped, aromatic leaves.
Large yellow or orange daisy heads, sometimes with many petal layers.
Branching leafy stems; check seed and foliage as well as flower color.
range: Mediterranean origin in the cited account; mostly encountered in cultivation.
season: Newly opened, healthy flower heads during the local growing season.
preparation: Identified petals add color to food. Use plants raised for culinary use.
caution: The common name marigold also refers to Tagetes. Ornamental nursery plants may have unsuitable pesticide treatments.

lookalikes.name: Tagetes marigolds
lookalikes.note: A shared common name does not make different genera interchangeable.

name: Wild garlic
summary: A spring woodland allium whose leaves are repeatedly confused with dangerous plants.
marks: Broad, lance-shaped leaves on individual stalks.
White star-shaped flowers in a cluster when flowering.
Garlic aroma is a supporting feature, never a sufficient test.
range: Shady, nutrient-rich European deciduous and mixed woodland; verify local occurrence.
season: Fresh leaves in local spring. Learn the whole plant in flower before attempting leaf gathering.
preparation: Only use leaves after expert-confirmed identification, checking every leaf separately.
caution: Lily of the valley and autumn crocus can grow among ramsons. Garlic scent transferred to hands can mislead.

lookalikes.name: Lily of the valley
lookalikes.note: Its leaves wrap a shared basal stalk; flowers are hanging bells.

lookalikes.name: Autumn crocus
lookalikes.note: Spring leaf clusters lack the autumn flowers. Mixed handfuls are dangerous.

stewardship: Clip individual leaves from abundant, permitted patches; leave bulbs in the soil.

name: Common purslane
summary: A low, fleshy warm-season plant with culinary use across many regions.
marks: Smooth, thick, succulent leaves clustered at joints.
Round, fleshy branching stems often tinged red.
Small yellow five-petaled flowers near shoot tips.
range: Cosmopolitan, with extensive human-assisted distribution.
season: Active succulent growth in warm conditions, often following rain or irrigation.
preparation: Confirmed leaves and stems are used raw or cooked as vegetables.
caution: Contains oxalates; avoid large intakes. Rule out spurges before any food use.

lookalikes.name: Spotted spurge
lookalikes.note: Spurge has thin, often hairy stems and irritating milky sap; purslane is fleshy.

stewardship: Gather from clean garden beds; leave surrounding vegetation and soil undisturbed.

name: Common chickweed
summary: A cool-season annual forming soft green patches with tiny, deeply divided white petals.
marks: Opposite, oval leaves with smooth margins.
A line of hairs along the otherwise soft stem.
Five white petals split deeply enough to resemble ten.
range: Eurasia and North Africa; introduced widely, including North America.
season: Cool, moist growing conditions; learn flowering plants before gathering tender shoots.
preparation: Correctly identified shoots have raw and lightly cooked food uses.
caution: Avoid mixing several groundcover species. Flowerless fragments are especially easy to confuse.

lookalikes.name: Scarlet pimpernel
lookalikes.note: This harmful lookalike has unnotched, usually orange-red or blue petals; consult a local key.

stewardship: Clip a few shoots rather than pulling mats from the soil.

marks: Three distinctly heart-shaped leaflets per leaf.
Small five-petaled yellow flowers.
Slender upright growth with elongated seed capsules.
range: North America and Eurasia in the cited account.
season: Identify flowering plants during active growth.
preparation: Documented as a tart food accent in small amounts, not as a bulk green.
caution: Large amounts can be harmful because of oxalates. Sour taste is never an identification test.

lookalikes.name: Clovers
lookalikes.note: Clover leaflets and dense pea-flower heads differ; check flowers and fruit as well as leaves.

stewardship: Leave flowers and capsules; avoid uprooting small plants.

marks: Basal leaves have two outward-pointing lobes near the base.
Slender ridged stalks carry tiny greenish or reddish flowers.
Leaves and flower stalks arise from a low perennial base.
range: Eurasian origin; widespread introductions.
season: Young leaves during fresh growth, after confirming the plant in flower.
preparation: A small culinary flavoring; avoid treating it as an unrestricted salad green.
caution: Contains substantial oxalic acid. Do not taste uncertain arrow-shaped leaves.

lookalikes.name: Arums
lookalikes.note: Poisonous arums can have arrow-shaped leaves; their fleshy flower spathes and leaf structure differ.

name: Garlic mustard
summary: A biennial with garlic-scented foliage and white cross-shaped flowers; invasive in some regions.
marks: First-year rounded leaves form a low rosette.
Second-year leaves become triangular and coarsely toothed.
Four white petals form a cross; narrow upright seed pods follow.
range: Native to Europe, parts of Asia and Africa; introduced in North America.
season: Young leaves before they become tough; flowering helps confirm identity.
preparation: Documented culinary use of young leaves in sauces and salads.
caution: A garlic smell alone cannot identify it. Do not spread mature seed during collection.

lookalikes.name: Other mustard rosettes
lookalikes.note: Confirm the four-petaled flowers and foliage before using young leaves.

stewardship: Follow local invasive-plant disposal advice; keep mature seed out of compost and new sites.

name: Cleavers
summary: A scrambling annual whose hooked hairs attach to neighboring plants and clothing.
marks: Narrow leaves in whorls of usually six to eight.
Weak four-sided stems with backward-pointing hooks.
Tiny white or greenish four-petaled flowers and bristly paired fruits.
range: Widespread in North America, Europe and northern Asia; native status varies.
season: Observe young shoots, flowers and hooked fruits through the local growing season.
preparation: Included for study; cooked shoots have documented use but rough hairs make raw gathering unsuitable.
caution: Other bedstraws differ chemically. Do not infer edibility from a sticky stem.

lookalikes.name: Other Galium
lookalikes.note: Confirm leaf-whorl counts, hooked hairs, flowers and fruit with a local key.

stewardship: Avoid pulling surrounding hedgerow plants when observing this scrambling species.

name: Fennel
summary: An aromatic Mediterranean herb with fine foliage and yellow umbels; wild identification needs particular care.
marks: Very finely divided, threadlike leaves.
Yellow flowers in large compound umbels.
Tall branching herb; aromatic foliage is supporting evidence only.
range: Mediterranean origin; naturalized around the world, sometimes invasive.
season: Confirm mature flowering plants; leafy growth and fully mature seeds are different collection stages.
preparation: Prefer a correctly named garden plant for culinary leaves and seeds.
caution: Carrot-family mistakes can be fatal. Do not gather an unknown umbellifer by smell.

name: Watercress

Seed pods have seeds in two rows per chamber; related watercresses differ.
range: European origin and introduced in North America; consult local floras elsewhere.
season: Learn flowering and fruiting plants; a green patch in flowing water is not evidence of safety.
preparation: Choose food-grown watercress from a controlled source rather than raw wild aquatic plants.
caution: Wild watercress can carry liver flukes and contaminants. Clear water and rinsing do not establish safety.

Persistent overlapping bracts remain after flowering.

Flowers on separate stalks; lateral petals commonly bear hairs.

summary: A creeping tropical herb with kidney-shaped leaves and documented regional food uses.

Long leaf stalks arise along creeping runners.
Small clustered flowers near the ground.
range: Tropical and subtropical Asia; the cited Singapore record lists regional native distribution.
season: Fresh healthy leaves during active moist-season growth; there is no universal northern calendar.
preparation: Leaves have food uses in parts of Asia. Prefer known cultivated material from clean soil.
caution: Wild wet-ground plants can be contaminated. Food use is not evidence for concentrated supplements or treatment claims.

name: Lemongrass
summary: A clump-forming tropical culinary grass with lemon-scented blades and thick overlapping leaf bases.
marks: Long straplike leaves with parallel veins.
Dense clumps; the apparent stalk is overlapping leaf sheaths.
Flowering is uncommon in cultivation.
range: Widely cultivated through the tropics; native origin is uncertain in the NParks account.
season: Active warm-season growth on an established cultivated clump.
preparation: Leaf blades flavor tea and broth; prepared leaf bases are used in cooking. Remove tough fibers as the recipe requires.
caution: Other Cymbopogon species are grown for fragrance or oils. A lemon scent does not make them interchangeable.

lookalikes.name: Citronella grasses
lookalikes.note: Use a correctly named culinary plant; young grasses are difficult to distinguish.

stewardship: Take a few outer shoots without uprooting the whole clump.

name: Roselle
summary: A tropical crop famous for tart red calyces. The familiar botanical name is Hibiscus sabdariffa.
marks: Upright reddish stems.
Mature leaves commonly have three to five lobes.
Hibiscus-like flowers with a dark center; fleshy calyces develop around fruit.
range: African origin; cultivated widely in tropical and subtropical regions.
season: Calyces after flowering while fleshy; timing depends on cultivar, day length and local climate.
preparation: Food-grown calyces are used in drinks and preserves. Follow a reliable recipe.
caution: Do not substitute ornamental hibiscus or identify by a red flower alone.

stewardship: Prefer cultivated plants and leave selected fruit for seed.

name: Moringa

Long, slender three-angled pods.
range: Indian origin; widely cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions.
season: Fresh leafy growth and tender immature pods during active growth.
preparation: Identified leaves are cooked as greens; immature pods have established culinary uses.
caution: This entry covers food parts only. Do not infer that roots, bark, extracts or water-treatment claims are safe.

name: Culantro
summary: A tropical seasoning herb with long toothed leaves, used in Caribbean, Latin American and Asian cooking.
marks: Long, smooth leaves in a basal rosette.
Finely toothed to spiny leaf edges.
Compact cylindrical greenish-white flower heads with pointed bracts.

season: Tender leaves before flowering makes them tougher; active growth can continue in humid tropical conditions.
preparation: Use leaves from a confirmed culinary plant as a seasoning.

Oil glands on foliage and largely hairless stems.

preparation: Documented culinary leaf use does not justify making concentrated tea, essential oil or medicinal extracts.

season: Healthy leaves during active growth on an established shrub.
preparation: Identified cultivated leaves have a documented herbal-tea and flavoring use.

name: Warrigal greens
summary: A sprawling coastal plant used as a cooked green, with preparation needed to reduce oxalic acid.
marks: Fleshy light-green leaves, oval to diamond-shaped.
Leaves have a velvety or granular-looking surface.
Low sprawling stems; confirm flowers and distinctive fruit with a local flora.

season: Healthy young leaves in active growth, often following rain in suitable climates.
preparation: Blanch identified leaves and discard the cooking water, following a reliable food recipe.
caution: Contains oxalic acid; do not present it as a raw salad green or unrestricted spinach substitute.

summary: A silvery Cape shrub with narrow aromatic leaves and woolly fruit heads; distinct from culinary rosemary.

Fluffy white fruit heads follow flowering.

Small yellow pea-family flowers.
Upright shrub; wild forms vary in growth and regeneration.
range: Southwestern South Africa, especially the Cederberg and neighboring mountain areas.
season: Cultivated crop timing follows local production practice, not a global monthly calendar.
preparation: Use traceable, prepared rooibos tea. Processing differs between green and oxidized products.
caution: Do not identify or harvest an unfamiliar fynbos shrub by needlelike leaves alone.

name: Poison hemlock
summary: A potentially fatal carrot-family plant that must be learned alongside edible-looking umbels.
marks: Smooth, hollow stems often marked with purple blotches.
Alternate, finely divided, roughly triangular leaves.
White flowers in compound umbels; first-year plants may have only a rosette.
range: European and Mediterranean origin; naturalized widely, including North America.
season: Hazard exists at every growth stage, including before flowers appear.
preparation: Do not eat, brew, taste or collect for the pantry.
caution: All parts are highly poisonous. Small amounts can be fatal; obtain urgent poison-service advice after exposure.

lookalikes.name: Fennel
lookalikes.note: Fennel has yellow umbels; young plants still require a full botanical key.

lookalikes.name: Common yarrow
lookalikes.note: Yarrow has miniature daisy heads, not true umbels.

stewardship: Keep a distance and report suspected plants to the local land manager; do not improvise removal.

name: Spotted water hemlock
summary: A highly poisonous North American wetland plant; other Cicuta species are also dangerous.
marks: Compound leaves with narrow, sharply toothed leaflets.
Leaflet veins commonly end in notches between the teeth.
White compound umbels and hollow, sometimes purple-marked stems.
range: North America; this profile does not cover all regional water hemlocks.
season: Dangerous throughout its life cycle; a nonflowering plant is still hazardous.
preparation: Do not eat or collect. Do not dig roots or cut stems to attempt identification.
caution: All parts are toxic and ingestion can be fatal. Seek urgent poison-service advice.

lookalikes.name: Other wetland umbels
lookalikes.note: Several edible-looking wetland plants resemble Cicuta. Habitat and one vein feature are insufficient.

lookalikes.name: Fennel
lookalikes.note: An aromatic herb name cannot rule out a poisonous umbellifer.

stewardship: Observe and photograph from a safe position; protect wetland soils.

name: Lily of the valley
summary: A poisonous woodland and garden plant whose spring leaves can be mixed with wild garlic.
marks: Broad parallel-veined leaves, usually paired around a shared basal stalk.
One-sided clusters of hanging white bell-shaped flowers.
Orange-red berries later in the season; flowers may be absent when leaves emerge.
range: Eurasian origin; cultivated and naturalized elsewhere.
season: Toxic in leaf, flower and fruit; spring leaf emergence is a key confusion period.
preparation: Do not eat, brew or add to gathered leaves.
caution: Can cause serious poisoning including heart-rhythm disturbances. Seek prompt poison-service advice after ingestion.

lookalikes.name: Wild garlic
lookalikes.note: Ramsons has star-shaped flowers, but leaves are often gathered before either plant flowers.

stewardship: Keep children and gathered food away from patches; avoid mixing handfuls of woodland leaves.

name: Autumn crocus
summary: A potentially fatal poisonous plant whose spring leaves appear separately from its autumn flowers.
marks: Clusters of broad leaves emerge in spring.
Pink to lilac flowers emerge without leaves later in the year.
Seasonally separated foliage and flowers make casual identification unreliable.
range: Central and southeastern Europe; also cultivated outside its native range.
season: Hazard in every season; spring leaves are an important wild-garlic lookalike.
preparation: Never eat, brew or substitute for saffron.
caution: Colchicine poisoning can be fatal and symptoms may be delayed. Do not wait for illness before seeking help.

lookalikes.note: Never gather mixed leaf clusters. A garlic smell on the hands can mask a mistaken leaf.

summary: A poisonous biennial often first seen as a low rosette, before its conspicuous flower spike develops.
marks: Coarse, wrinkled, hairy leaves in a first-year rosette.
Alternate smaller leaves on the later flowering stem.
Tall spikes of hanging tubular flowers, often internally spotted.

season: The leaf-only rosette is dangerous as well as the flowering plant.
preparation: Do not eat, brew or use in home remedies.
caution: Cardiac glycosides can cause serious, potentially fatal poisoning. Seek urgent advice after ingestion.

season: Treat every stage as unsuitable for food gathering.
preparation: Do not make tea, ingest essential oil or use as a home remedy.
